newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa seen relaxing fx rules for funds further.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa seen relaxing fx rules for funds further.

text.p: South African authorities are likely to increase the amount of funds institutions can hold offshore if market conditions remain favourable, according to Selwyn Feldman, chairman of the Association of Unit Trusts.
At present local pension funds, insurance companies and unit trusts (mutual funds) are limited to holding 10 percent of their assets overseas.
But Feldman, who is also managing director of Old Mutual Unit Trusts, said this ceiling would soon be hit by his company and others in the industry.
"I think if we ask for 15 or 20 percent we will probably get it. But we've got to catch the authorities at the right moment," he told reporters after a presentation.

Feldman said his preference was to do away with all restrictions, particularly since outflows were in any case being conducted via asset swaps with foreign counterparties which ensured they were reserve neutral.
But he said the government was likely to continue to adopt a cautious approach to this aspect of relaxing exchange controls. He declined to predict how soon the next relaxation was likely to occur.
The authorities have been moving slowly to free up restrictions on local fund managers over the last two years.

For the unit trust industry, the March 12 budget offered a major step forward by allowing them to invest up to 10 percent of their total assets abroad and not, as before, 10 percent of each individual mutual fund.

Feldman said officials had argued in the past that there was no need to increase the offshore allowance since companies had not fully utilised the 10 percent concession. But the extra flexibility given in the budget meant that unit trusts would soon be banging up against this ceiling.

"In the case of Old Mutual we think we will get to the 10 percent level in the next month or two...most management companies will also use the limit to the full and that will put on pressure for a higher limit," he said.
Jeremy Bolton, portfolio manager of Old Mutual Investors Fund, said increased offshore exposure made sense in order to diversify risk and seek new opportunities for clients.
But Old Mutual, the country's largest investment group, was still likely to remain invested primarily in South Africa even after exchange controls were scrapped.
"I'd be surprised if it goes much above 20 percent for Old Mutual as a whole," Bolton said.
He added that the Reserve Bank, by requiring funds to use asset swaps which it must approve, had effectively created a "tap" mechanism with which it could control outflows.
The ease with which asset swaps were approved and the conditions under which they were granted often varied, he said.
"I think they (the Reserve Bank) are playing a balancing act...The goalposts seem to change week by week."

Feldman said Old Mutual Unit Trusts had increased its total offshore holdings to 558 million rand at the end of March from 233 million at the end of 1996, out of a total allowance under the 10 percent rule of 970 million.
The unit trust industry's overall asset base at the end of last year was 43.8 billion rand, of which Old Mutual accounted for 9.7 billion rand.
